cues.text: A Relic and a Legend
The Basilica of the Holy Blood in Bruges, Belgium, houses one of medieval Europe's most venerated relics.
It is a small rock-crystal vial said to contain a cloth stained with the Blood of Christ, traditionally attributed to Joseph of Arimathea.
According to the Gospels, Joseph prepared Christ's body for burial.

Popular legend, first recorded by a fourteenth-century chronicler not always known for careful accuracy, held that the relic was brought to Bruges in 1150 by Thierry of Alsace, Count of Flanders, returning from the Second Crusade.
What the Documents Actually Show
Modern historians have found this account difficult to sustain.
No record places the relic in Bruges anywhere in the twelfth century, and the earliest surviving document that actually mentions it dates only to 1256.
Most scholars today believe the relic more likely reached Bruges after the sack of Constantinople in 1204, during the Fourth Crusade.
Crusaders including Baldwin IX, Count of Flanders, brought it back among a great wave of relics looted from the Byzantine imperial collection.
This entry follows that more widely supported dating rather than the traditional legend.
A Procession Nearly Eight Centuries Old
Whatever its precise path to Flanders, the relic's veneration at Bruges is itself of genuine antiquity.
The city's guilds are recorded processing with it as early as 1291.
The Procession of the Holy Blood is still held every year on Ascension Day.
The relic is carried through the streets by bishops and prelates before thousands of participants, and the procession is counted among Europe's oldest continuously observed religious processions.
Legacy
We find in Bruges's Holy Blood something common to several of the Precious Blood relics venerated across medieval Europe.
Its antiquity and sincerity are not in question, even where the precise legend explaining its arrival has not withstood historical scrutiny.
Rather than choosing between skepticism and credulity, the fair-minded response is to hold both truths together.
A community's eight centuries of genuine reverence stand alongside a documentary record asking us to receive the relic's traditional origin story as pious legend rather than settled fact.
